The Nijubashi Bridge, an iconic double-arched stone and steel structure, marks the main entrance to Tokyo's Imperial Palace. While the name "Nijubashi" (meaning "Double Bridge") originally referred to an older wooden structure, it now commonly refers to the two bridges spanning the moat: the stone Meganebashi ("Eyeglass Bridge") and the steel Seimon Tetsubashi (Imperial Palace Main Gate Iron Bridge). . #SlowLiving  #instagood  #instamood  #fyp  #instagram  #trip  #travelgram  #travel #jalanjalan  #10000steps  #walk #walking  #alley #dinner #jepang #japan #budget #hiyoshi #tokyo #yokohama #castle  created by Alex with Alex's original sound - Alex

🇯🇵The Nijubashi Bridge is one of the most iconic landmarks at the Tokyo Imperial Palace, but there’s a secret that makes it even more fascinating than most people realize.The name “Nijubashi” literally means “Double Bridge,” but the catch is that it isn’t actually two bridges. The term comes from the reflection of the bridge in the water, which creates the illusion of a second bridge, giving the structure its name. This makes the Nijubashi Bridge incredibly photogenic, as visitors often capture the stunning double reflection in the moat surrounding the palace.But that’s not the only secret behind this historic bridge.The bridge itself has deep historical significance. Originally, it wasn’t just a beautiful piece of architecture; it served as the main entrance to the Imperial Palace for officials and dignitaries in the past. The bridge has stood through centuries of Japanese history, including the Edo period and World War II, where the area surrounding the Palace was rebuilt.Interestingly, the Nijubashi is not just a visual masterpiece; it symbolizes the connection between the palace’s royal family and the people of Japan. Although the bridge is accessible to the public, it’s also a reminder of the exclusivity and the secretive nature of the palace grounds, which are usually off-limits to most visitors.Many visitors might walk across it without realizing the deeper meaning behind the bridge’s construction or its historical role in Japan’s royal legacy. So the next time you find yourself standing on the Nijubashi Bridge, take a moment to appreciate the hidden history beneath the surface—the reflection in the water might just be the perfect metaphor for the stories that have been reflected in the history of the Imperial Palace itself.  #nijubashibridge  #tokyoimperialpalace  #reelsviralシ #highlightseveryone #highlightseveryonefollowers2025 #reelstrending #trendingreelsvideo #foryouシ #justforyou #japantravel #tokyotraveltips #tokyotravelguide #tokyo  #japan  #travelfacts #photography #travel  #architecturelovers  #bridge  #japantrip #TokyoAdventures #TokyoDreams #TokyoLife #TokyoMagic  created by JapanSuki🇯🇵 with Rourourourous's わたしからあなたへ

Stop just visiting random shrines. Come to the place where the samurai were truly born. ⚔️⛩️ This is Tsurugaoka Hachimangu — the spiritual heart of Kamakura, Japan’s first samurai capital. Here’s what makes it different: 	1.	This was Minamoto no Yoritomo’s sacred ground — the man who founded Japan’s first shogunate. 	2.	Look at the ponds: one is designed with 3 islands (victory)… the other with 4 (death). A quiet symbol of an old conflict. 	3.	The main approach is epic — it runs straight through the city, aligned from the sea like a ceremonial runway. ⚠️ Pro tip: Don’t just stay at the bottom. Climb the grand stairway for a breathtaking view over Kamakura. Kotoku-in Temple is a small yet powerful temple in Kamakura, best known for housing the iconic Great Buddha (Daibutsu). Cast in the 13th century, the massive bronze statue has stood outdoors for centuries, surviving earthquakes and storms with quiet resilience. Hasedera Temple has been sitting in the hills of Kamakura since the Nara period, with a massive wooden Kannon statue and some of the best sea views in town. But once late May rolls around, things shift — the hillside Ajisai Path fills with over 2,500 hydrangeas (40+ varieties!), and thanks to the alkaline soil here, the blooms turn into these incredible shades of blue, purple, and soft pink you don't really see anywhere else. It's easily one of the most photographed hydrangea spots in Japan, and once you've seen it in person, it's easy to understand why. Planning a visit? Here's what you need to know 👇 📍 3-11-2 Hase, Kamakura — just a 5-min walk from Hase Station (Enoden line) 🕐 8:00–17:00 (slightly extended during hydrangea season) 📌 Bloom season: late May to late June, with peak usually mid-to-late June 📌 General admission: ¥400 adults / ¥200 elementary students 📌 Hydrangea Path ticket: an extra ¥500 timed-entry ticket is required during peak bloom — book online in advance, slots go fast 📌 Don't miss: Miharashidai lookout for panoramic views of Kamakura town, Yuigahama Beach & the Shonan coast 📌 Pro tip: arrive right at opening or visit on a rainy day; the colors actually look more vivid in the rain, and the crowds are thinner Have you ever chased hydrangea season in Japan? #japan #tokyo #japantrip #japantravel #traveljapan  created by tinaH_travel with 山口夕依's She Share Story (for Vlog)

🍁 Sankei-en Garden - Kanagawa Elegant autumn foliage at the classic Japanese garden 🏞️ Sankei-en Garden is a traditional Japanese garden in Yokohama, designed and built by Hara Sankei. Many historically valuable buildings have been relocated from Kyoto and Kamakura to the vast grounds. 👟When you enter the garden, there is a large pond at the center, and you can take a leisurely stroll around it. During the autumn season, the promenade at the backside is open. It is a must see spot for the beautifully colored trees along the river decorating the historical buildings. This is surely an experience to enjoy a typical Japanese autumn scene. ✨The particularly eye-catching “three-story pagoda,” rising from a small hill, is the oldest structure in the garden. It is positioned so that it can be beautifully viewed from anywhere in the garden, making it a symbol. 🇯🇵Since this garden is such a great place to experience traditional Japanese culture, it is extremely popular with foreign visitors. In the autumn season, the gardens are lit up, creating a different, fantastical view at night. 💍📸It's also a popular spot for pre-wedding photo shoots. There were many newlyweds in traditional Japanese attire and their families enjoying their day. 📅Visited 12/Dec/2024 📍 Sankei-en Garden - Kanagawa (三溪園 – 神奈川) 🚗1.5 hours from central Tokyo 🚃🚌JR Negishi Station to Yokohama Municipal Bus "Honmoku Bus Stop" → 10 minute walk Address: 58-1 Honmoku Sannotani, Naka-ku, Yokohama, Kanagawa 231-0824 Parking: 60 spaces availavle (1000 yen for up to 2 hours, 200 yen for every 30 minutes thereafter) 🕐Opening hours： 9am - 5pm Closed: December 26 to 31th Admission: Adults 700 yen / Child 400 yen (14 years old and below) 🍁Autumn leaves: Late November to mid-December 🎧✨Hotaru “Declining Sun” #Hotaru #SankeienGarden #Kanagawa #Sankeien #JapaneseGarden #Traditional #Yokohama #三溪園 created by Hotaru ⛩️JAPAN TRAVEL⛩️ with Hotaru's Declining Sun

One of the coolest museums I’ve visited 🍜 The Shin-Yokohama Museum in Japan is one of the most fun museums I’ve ever visited. The first floor explains everything about the origins and the history of Ramen as well as explaining everything about different soup bases, tare and different regional Ramen and Ramen varieties. And you can even make your own Ramen here! The B1 and B2 floor consists of a food hall where you can actually try many different Ramen flavors from popular individual shops. Walk down Takeshita Street, and then turn left onto Cat Street, which is just a short walk away. Owakudani is an active volcanic valley in Hakone, famous for its steaming vents and the legendary black ‘kuro-tamago’ (boiled in sulfurous water).  The most scenic access is via the Hakone Ropeway — typically:  Hakone-Yumoto → (bus/boat) → Togendai → Ropeway → Owakudani, or via the Hakone Tozan Cablecar to Sounzan then ropeway.  Note: the ropeway/park can close or require reservations when volcanic gas levels are high — check status before you go. 大涌谷は箱根にある活火山地帯で、噴煙を上げる噴気孔や、硫黄泉で茹でた名物の黒い卵「黒たまご」で有名です。最も景色を楽しめるアクセス方法は箱根ロープウェイを利用することです。一般的なルートは、箱根湯本駅→（バスまたは遊覧船）→桃源台→ロープウェイ→大涌谷、または箱根登山ケーブルカーで早雲山駅まで行き、そこからロープウェイに乗るルートです。なお、火山ガスの濃度が高い場合は、ロープウェイや周辺施設が閉鎖されたり、事前予約が必要となる場合がありますので、お出かけ前に運行状況をご確認ください #tokyo #volcano #foryou #fyp   #creatorsearchinsights created by 🎌 𝐋𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐢𝐧 𝒥𝒶𝓅𝒶𝓃 🎌 with Adrián Berenguer's Little Things

The Inubosaki Lighthouse is one of my favorite hidden gems found on the Chiba coast. It was constructed in 1874 and is listed on the International Association of Marine Aids to Navigation and Lighthouse Authorities’ “100 lighthouses in the world that are historic and architectural monuments.” Take the stairs to the top for a panoramic view of Cape Inubo and the Pacific Ocean, and then stop by the “INUBOW TERASU TERRACE '' market for some dining and shopping. The lighthouse is about a 10-minute walk from Inubo Station on the Choshi Electric Railway.  The Choshi Electric Railway can be accessed by transferring at JR Choshi Station, which can be reached in less than 2 hours from Tokyo by limited-express train.  #chiba #千葉 #visitchiba #beyondtokyo #lighthouse #oceanview created by Visit Chiba | Beyond Tokyo with Track and Field's Back In Your Life (Instrumental)

Sunflower Fields at Mangan-ji Temple, Choshi City, Chiba Come August, the grounds in front of Mangan-ji Temple are transformed into an idyllic Japanese summer scene thanks to these fields of towering sunflowers. Katori Jingu Shrine is located in Chiba Prefecture and stands as one of Japan’s most ancient and prestigious sacred sites. ⛩️ ​With a history spanning over 2,600 years, this magnificent shrine enshrines "Futsunushi no Ookami," the legendary deity of martial arts, swordsmanship, and divine power.  ​It holds the absolute highest status in Japanese shrine hierarchy. It is honored as the "Ichinomiya" (the highest-ranking shrine) of ancient Shimosa Province, historically designated as a "Kanpei Taisha" (Grand Imperial Shrine), and is one of the rare "Chokuraisha"—a select group of elite shrines that receive special envoys directly sent by the Emperor of Japan for sacred rituals.  ​Walking down the majestic, lantern-lined path surrounded by giant cedar trees, you can feel the deep, awe-inspiring spiritual energy that has protected this land since antiquity. 🌿 #KatoriJingu #JapanTravel #Chiba #Shrine  created by The Hearts of Japan with The Hearts of Japan's オリジナル楽曲 - The Hearts of Japan

📍Chiba 🇯🇵 Katori Jingu Shrine, established in 643 BC, it’s one of the few shrines honored with the prestigious title “Jingu.” Here stands the legendary Kaname-Ishi (要石) — the “keystone” said to pierce deep into the earth to pin down the giant catfish that causes earthquakes, protecting the land ⛩️ The shrine grounds are breathtaking: the main hall (honden) and tower gate (rōmon) date back to 1700 (Genroku era), built under Tokugawa Tsunayoshi. With their black-lacquered roof, vivid vermilion gate, and timeless architecture, they’re absolutely stunning ✨ Don’t miss the sacred giant camphor tree, about 1,000 years old with a 10-meter trunk, truly awe-inspiring 🥰 I prayed, drew a fortune, and picked up the Kaname-Ishi omamori (lucky charm) 🍀 Such a wonderful experience!! 🥹 Are you a fan of Suzume no Tojimari? Most people know the story of Hachiko, the loyal dog who continued waiting for his owner every day for nearly 10 years after he suddenly passed away at work. But did you know there’s also a touching reunion statue hidden at the University of Tokyo? Hachiko’s owner, Hidesaburo Ueno, was actually a professor at the University of Tokyo, which is why the Hongo Campus features a beautiful statue of the two finally reuniting. Surrounded by historic architecture and lush greenery, it’s one of Tokyo’s most heartwarming hidden spots. 💕 Would you visit this statue on your next trip to Tokyo? 🇯🇵 📍1 Chome-1-1 Yayoi, Bunkyo City, Tokyo  #hachiko #traveltokyo #dog created by mytokyolife with Minaco's Ghibli style, Japanese beauty, fireworks, piano solo(1585174)

Aberdeen’s very own Chambers of Secrets  The Town House on Union Street is one of Aberdeen’s most impressive buildings built in the 1870s, with gothic towers, chandeliers in almost every room, and even a statue of Queen Victoria unveiled in 1863. But for me, it’s more than history. I was back here recently, and it brought back memories of 2012, when the Town House hosted celebrations for the London Olympics torch relay. I had the honour of being one of the torchbearers that day and standing here again reminded me how much pride this building has witnessed over the years. It’s easy to walk past without looking up, but the Town House is a place where Aberdeen’s history and celebrations come together. #Aberdeen #AberdeenHistory #TownHouse #UnionStreet #GraniteCity  created by TokOfTheDeen | Lesley-Ann with Mark Fabian & Alexander Smith's Magical Mystery

*Invite* I was invited earlier in the week to @Town House Aberdeen to sample their new menu. What you have is 2 courses for £20, 3 for £25 and a range of cocktails at 8 pound a pop. If you don't fancy a massive meal then you also have the option of three of the small plates for £15.  What we had: Cheese Croquettes (small plate) Calamari (small plate) Salmon Fillet  Buttermilk Chicken Burger Sticky Toffee Pudding Old Fashioned Cocktail  Bramble Cocktail  Espresso Martini  Margarita Mocktail  All the food was well presented and tasted great. The "small" plates are of a very good size and quality, and the mains were delicious. The cocktails were pleasing both in taste and visually and even the mocktails were tasty. None of us had ANY criticism of the food or drinks at all and the small but perfectly formed menu is superb value.  The dining area itself is lovely, airy and elegant and when paired with the superb service it made for a fantastic dining experience. The Townhouse wasn't on my radar before, but it comes with a full recommendation from me, and it left quite the impression!  Make sure you check it out (down the side of the Music Hall) and tell them I sent you! We’ll cross that bridge when we come to it… well, we’re here  The Brig o’ Balgownie in Old Aberdeen dates back to around the 1300s and is one of the oldest surviving bridges in Scotland. For centuries, this was the main way to cross the River Don, making it a key route for trade, travel and movement through the north-east. There’s even debate over who built it with some crediting Robert the Bruce and others Bishop Henry Cheyne. Built in a single Gothic arch from granite and sandstone, it stood as the main northern route until the 1800s. Now it’s one of the most peaceful spots in Aberdeen… but it’s seen more history than most places in the city. 📍 Old Aberdeen 🚶‍♀️ River Don walk 🏰 Historic Aberdeen Did you know this? 👇 created by TokOfTheDeen | Lesley-Ann with Ofyra's Fenc Rap Beats

Castle Fraser is one of Scotland's largest and most elaborate baronial tower houses, located near Kemnay in Aberdeenshire. Managed by the National Trust for Scotland, this spectacular Z-plan stronghold features a fairy-tale silhouette of turrets, gables, and secret chambers dating back as far as 1450. It is famously home to quirky historical features like the Laird’s Lug (a secret listening hole) and even a resident's wooden leg from the Napoleonic Wars. Hidden Features: Discover secret staircases, hidden trapdoors, and spy holes used by the Lairds to monitor guests in the Great Hall. Estate & Gardens: The castle sits on 120 hectares of grounds including a beautiful 18th-century walled garden, woodland trails like Miss Bristow’s Trail, and a children's play area. Ghostly Legends: It is reputedly haunted by the "Green Lady," a princess supposedly murdered in the Round Tower, and a "lady in black". #magicalplaces #scotland #scottishcastles #explorescotland #foryoupagе  created by Moss Fairy with The Poet's love story

Step inside one of Aberdeen’s greatest treasures the David Welch Winter Gardens at Duthie Park. Opened in 1899 and lovingly restored after storm damage in the 1960s, the Winter Gardens are now one of the largest indoor plant collections in Europe. From towering tropical palms to cacti and succulents and of course the famous giant frog it’s a space every Aberdonian knows and loves. But once a year, the Winter Gardens transform after dark into something truly magical. The Winter Wonder Wander, organised by Friends of Duthie Park, turns the park and gardens into a spectacular winter light trail. The 2025 event runs from the 4th to the 11th of November, and while tickets are nearly sold out, a few are still available – don’t miss your chance! Whether you’re discovering the history of Duthie Park, planning a family trip to the Winter Gardens, or looking for Christmas events in Aberdeen, this video will give you a glimpse of both the year-round beauty of the gardens and the festive magic of the Winter Wonder Wander. 📍 Location: Duthie Park, Aberdeen, Scotland 🎟️ Event: Winter Wonder Wander, run by Friends of Duthie Park created by TokOfTheDeen | Lesley-Ann with SharpFourStudio's Fun and Upbeat Pop Rock

A tropical jungle in Scotland  Most people have no idea this place even exists. Hidden inside Aberdeen, the David Welch Winter Gardens is actually one of the largest indoor gardens in Europe and it’s completely free to visit. But here’s the wild part… The original glasshouses were destroyed by storms in 1969 and had to be demolished. Just one year later, it was rebuilt bigger and better and now it’s home to plants from all over the world, from deserts to tropical rainforests. There’s even a Japanese garden inside. It feels like stepping into another country without leaving Scotland. It’s a place that has hosted legends: Mary, Queen of Scots, famously stayed here for three days following the Battle of Corrichie in 1562. Her bedchamber still stands as a silent witness to that visit." ​"But it wasn't always a place of royal visits. It has seen the chaos of the Battle of Bannockburn, the turmoil of the Covenanter wars, and even served as barracks for troops returning from the beaches of Dunkirk during the Second World War." ​(The Near-Death Experience) "By the mid-20th century, the castle was a hollow shell—ridden with dry rot, missing its roof, and left to crumble. Many declared it beyond saving. But then came Captain John Hay of Delgatie. Driven by a fierce determination, he took on the 'impossible' task of restoring the ruins, transforming a decaying relic back into a living, breathing home." ​(The Present: Alive and Thriving) "Today, Delgatie Castle is more than just a monument—it is a thriving Clan Hay Centre and a 4-star destination. I’m always surprised when I discover somewhere new in Scotland. We travel around quite a bit, so you’d think by now I’ve seen most places… but then you find somewhere like this. Drum Castle really surprised me. It’s just outside Aberdeen near Banchory, and somehow it had never been on my radar until now. The Royal Forest and Tower of Drum were gifted to the Irvine family by Robert the Bruce in 1323, and the family lived here for more than 650 years. Later, a Jacobean mansion house was added, and during the Victorian era the lower hall was transformed into a library, now home to over 4,000 books. Episode 224 - Fyvie Castle is located in Aberdeenshire and it is an 800 year old Scottish Baronial fortress. It features five distinct towers that were added by different families, a renowned collection of Raeburn portraits, a historic tennis court and being famous for its haunting legends and reported curses. Records indicate it was a royal stronghold as early as the year 1211 under King William the Lion. Famous Guests, such as Robert the Bruce, held an open-air court here and Charles the 1st spent part of his childhood at the castle. Fyvie castle has five distinct towers, each built by one of the five successive families that owned it. Preston, Meldrum, Seton, Gordon, and Forbes-Leith. In 1644, the castle was occupied by the Marquis of Montrose, who successfully defended it against the Covenanter army. The castle was then transformed from a medieval fortress into a luxurious Edwardian home in the late 19th century by Alexander Leith, the 1st Lord Leith of Fyvie. Legend says the seer Thomas the Rhymer cursed the castle after being denied shelter, resulting in a curse where the castle would never pass in a direct line of inheritance for more than two generations. A stone with the same curse is located at the castle and it is said to remain permanently damp, regardless of weather. During the 1920 renovations, a female skeleton was discovered behind a bedroom wall, which was believed to be Lady Meldrum, who died around the year 1400. I didn’t realise this park used to be someone’s house. Before it was one of Aberdeen’s most loved green spaces, Hazlehead Park was once a private estate. Hazlehead Park gets its name from Hazlehead House a 17th-century mansion that stood here for centuries, owned by prominent Aberdeen families. This wasn’t somewhere you’d wander through for fresh air or a Sunday stroll. In the early 1900s, the land was bought by the city and opened up for public use. The house itself didn’t survive, but the name did and so did the land. Now it’s a place for dog walks, fresh air, childhood memories and quiet moments. The Linn of Dee is a famous natural beauty spot in Aberdeenshire, Scotland, where the powerful River Dee narrows drastically to rush through a 300-metre natural rock gorge. Managed by the National Trust for Scotland as part of the spectacular Mar Lodge Estate, this landmark sits at the edge of the Cairngorms National Park. It was famously favoured as a picnic spot by Queen Victoria, who personally opened the iconic Gothic-style stone bridge spanning the chasm in 1857. Today, it serves as both a tranquil destination for short woodland walks and the primary gateway for serious hiking expeditions into the high Cairngorm plateau. 📣 “I have an announcement…” Ever wondered how Aberdeen got its news before Social Media and Fubar? Back in 1686, the Mercat Cross was the city’s original news feed. Royal proclamations, new laws, market days, even death sentences were all read aloud here in the Castlegate, with crowds gathering to hear the latest updates. The cross itself is a masterpiece sixteen stone columns, carved medallions of Scottish monarchs, and a unicorn on top watching over the square. What an incredible privilege to be invited for an exclusive behind the scenes tour of Aberdeen Football Club and the iconic Pittodrie Stadium. ❤️⚪  Founded in 1903, Aberdeen FC is one of Scotland’s most successful football clubs, with a proud history that stretches back more than 120 years.  Walking through the stadium, it was impossible not to reflect on the countless memories created here from dramatic league matches and cup finals to unforgettable European nights. ⚽ Pittodrie has been Aberdeen’s home since 1903. 🏟️ It became the first all-seated stadium in Great Britain in 1978, years ahead of many other major grounds. 🌍 Aberdeen remain the only Scottish club to have won two European trophies — the 1983 European Cup Winners’ Cup and the 1983 European Super Cup. 🏆 The famous 1983 side, managed by Sir Alex Ferguson, defeated Real Madrid 2–1 in Gothenburg before going on to beat Hamburg to become champions of Europe once again. 🔴 And in another remarkable achievement, Aberdeen have been a top flight club since 1905 without relegation, a testament to the club’s consistency and support over the decades!  From the dressing rooms and tunnel to the stands and pitchside views, this tour offered a fascinating glimpse into the heart of a club that means so much to the city and its people.  As someone who loves sharing the stories that make Aberdeen unique, it was a genuinely special experience to learn more about the history, achievements and legacy of the Dons. A huge thank you to everyone at Aberdeen FC for the warm welcome and for sharing the stories behind this iconic stadium. You won’t like this… but you should know it. This is Powis Gateway in Old Aberdeen. Most people walk straight through it without a second thought but this landmark was built using wealth connected to the transatlantic slave trade. Powis Gateway was constructed in 1833–1834 as the grand entrance to the Powis Estate, commissioned by the Leslie family of Powis. Members of the family owned plantations in Jamaica, where enslaved African people were forced to work under brutal conditions. When slavery was abolished in 1834, plantation-owning families across Britain received financial compensation from the government for the loss of enslaved labour. The enslaved people themselves received nothing. That wealth fed back into estates and developments in Scotland, including buildings like this one. This isn’t about tearing history down. It’s about understanding it properly. Aberdeen’s past is proud, complicated, and global and places like this remind us that some of our history is hidden in plain sight. They came from every corner of Europe to kneel here. Kings sought its blessing. Above the North Sea stood the Cathedral of St Andrews, the largest church Scotland ever built. Within its walls were believed to rest the relics of Saint Andrew, Scotland's patron saint. For centuries, this was the spiritual heart of Scotland. Then everything changed. In 1559, the Scottish Reformation reached St Andrews. The cathedral was attacked, abandoned, and slowly dismantled. Not by a foreign army. Not by an invading king. The destruction came from within. Stone by stone, this sacred place became a ruin. Today, millions know St Andrews for golf. But long before the fairways, this was the spiritual heart of Scotland. The King held an engagement in Aberdeen, where he is to met a 99-year-old D-Day veteran at a regimental museum. Charles is visiting The Gordon Highlanders Museum, which celebrates the story of the British regiment originally raised by the 5th Duke of Gordon in 1784. As the Duke of Rothesay, Charles was appointed Colonel in Chief of the regiment in 1978 and remained so until its amalgamation with the Queen’s Own Highlanders in 1994. During this time, Charles visited the regiment’s 1st Battalion on operations – while they were training in the field – and in barracks. As well as viewing recent renovations at the museum and meeting some of the staff involved, the King met museum volunteers and supporters, among them 99-year-old D-Day veteran Jim Gleannie. The veteran of the Gordon Highlanders was unable to join last summer’s D-Day commemorations in Normandy. The engagement on Monday marks the King’s first visit to the museum since 2011, when he went there after unveiling the Gordon Highlanders statue in the city’s Castlegate. #news #royals #update #stvnews #aberdeen #royalfamily  created by STV News with STV News's original sound

Tolbooth Museum The Tolbooth Museum is one of the oldest buildings in Aberdeen, Scotland, with a history dating back to the 17th century. It was originally built in 1615 as a tollbooth, meaning it served as a courthouse and prison. At that time, it was used to hold criminals, debtors, and political prisoners. The building is located on Castle Street, an important historical area in Aberdeen. Inside, prisoners were kept in very small and dark cells, often in harsh conditions. Some prisoners were even chained or forced to wear heavy iron collars. During the 18th and early 19th centuries, the Tolbooth continued to be used as a jail and played a role during events like the Jacobite uprisings, when supporters were imprisoned there. In the 19th century, the building stopped being used as a prison. Because of its historical importance, it was preserved instead of being demolished. Later, in the 20th century, it was turned into a museum. Today, the Tolbooth Museum is an important historical site that tells the story of crime and punishment in the past. However, it is currently closed to the public, although it remains a significant landmark in Aberdeen’s history.#VisitScotland #aberdeen  created by Soran with MAICO's Pure Love (Instrumental)

Tolquhon Castle is a substantial ruinous courtyard castle with a large tower and some fantastic stone carving on the gatehouse, held by the Preston family and then by the Forbeses, in a quiet spot near Tarves (Tarves Tomb) in Aberdeenshire in northeast Scotland. Once a strong but comfortable fortress and now an atmospheric ruin, Tolquhon Castle consists of a strong ruined 15th-century tower (known as the Preston Tower) in one corner of a courtyard enclosed by ranges of buildings, including a drum-towered gatehouse. A large round tower stands at one corner of the courtyard, with a square tower at the opposite side. The walls are pierced by gunloops. The main three-storey block, opposite the tower, has a projecting semi-circular stair-tower crowned by a square caphouse. This part of the castle was built for Sir William Forbes, 7th laird of Tolquhon, but the master builder Thomas Leiper, whose initials are on the outside of the building.  #tolquhoncastle #ellon #aberdeenshire #scotland #scotlandtiktok  created by Hayley 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿 with zonamusik90an's Scorpions Wind of Change

Have you ever been to Castle Menzies? (pronounced Mingis) A 16th-century castle that sits just round the corner from Aberfeldy and was the seat of the Chief of Clan Menzies for 500 years.  If you're not sure what a "Clan" is, the word essentially means "chidren of", so if you were part of clan Menzies, you were the children of Menzies. Now, that's not to say you had the second name Menzies, as you may have just lived on their land, or were part of a sept family (like Murdochs are to Macphersons), but you owed loyatly to that Chief. And usually some form of tax too...often whisky 🥃 Be sure to save this post and add Castle Menzies to your list of castles to tour in Scotland! It even hosted Bonnie Prince Charlie and the Duke of Cumberland in the run-up to the Battle of Culloden in 1746. #tartanviking #highlander #meninkilts #scotland #visitscotland #scotlandtiktok #tiktokscotland #scottishtiktok #scotlandtravel #travelscotland #scotlandadventures #outlander #bloodofmyblood  created by TartanViking with Naleef's original sound

Wades Bridge, Aberfeldy, Scotland. # Wade's Bridge (originally known as Tay Bridge) is five-arch bridge crossing the River Tay at Aberfeldy, Perth and Kinross, Scotland. A Category A listed structure built in 1733,[1] to a design by William Adam, it carries the pedestrian and vehicle traffic of Poplar Avenue.[2] Erected for the Board of Ordnance, to the order of Lieutenant General George Wade, its original purpose was as a military road linking the garrisons at Ruthven, Fort George, Fort Augustus and Fort William.#scotland #history #aberfeldy #arielphotography #dronevideo #wadesbridge created by DFD_Photography with Mauro Rawn's Scotland

Following on from Old Monkland Parish Church, this drone footage takes us to New Monkland Parish Church in Glenmavis, a village on the outskirts of Airdrie. Built during the 19th century, this church served growing industrial communities linked to coal mining, quarries, and ironworks across the Monklands. As the population spread beyond Old Monkland, New Monkland became the spiritual heart of working families who shaped the area through labour and industry. The church and graveyard tell the story of Glenmavis’s role in the industrial rise of Airdrie and Coatbridge — from long shifts underground to lives rooted in tight-knit communities. From medieval Old Monkland to industrial New Monkland, this is the next chapter in the Monklands story. 👇 Did you know this history — or have family connections to Glenmavis? caption: Let your kids take a little trip down memory lane this week at Summerlee Museum of Scottish Industrial Life. It is such a fun and educational place for a family day out, especially if your children love discovering new things. One of the most exciting parts is seeing the beautiful cottage-style homes and learning how traditional Scottish homes looked many years ago. Children can see how everyday things like televisions, washing machines, fridges, hair dryers and other household items looked decades ago. It is history, but in a way that feels real, fun and easy for kids to understand. Summerlee is also a great choice for both sunny and rainy days. There is plenty to explore indoors, plus a playground and open spaces where children can run around, play and enjoy themselves. Save this for your next family day out, and tag us if you visit! Rainbow Bridge In Alexandria , Scotland, the " Rainbow Bridge " is the local nickname for the  Bonhill Bridge , which spans the River Leven.  The River Leven: The bridge carries traffic across the River Leven, the only outlet of Loch Lomond. Historical Sandstone Pyramids: On the Alexandria side of the bridge, there are three red sandstone pyramids. These were built using the remains of the piers from the previous 1898 bridge. Gas Light Remains: Situated behind these pyramids are the remains of four gas lights that originally stood on the piers of the older 1898 bridge. Memorial Plaque: One of the pyramids incorporates the original commemorative plaque from the opening of the 1898 bridge.  Key Bridge Facts Name: Formally the  Bonhill Bridge , it earned its nickname due to its steel tied-through arch design. Opened: It was completed on 28 July 1987, replacing a 19th-century steel "Whipple Arch" bridge. Christie Park,  Alexandria, West Dunbartonshire, Scotland Christie Park is a historic community park in the heart of Alexandria, West Dunbartonshire, covering approximately 14 acres of formal gardens and wilder woodland. History Establishment: Opened on 5th July 1902, the park was formerly known as Notman's Park. The "Bonus" Park: It was gifted to the inhabitants of the Parish of Bonhill by John Christie, an owner of the Alexandria Works. Locally, it was often called the "Bonus Park" because the funds used for its development were allegedly redirected from the workers' annual bonuses. Key Features: The park includes a War Memorial (unveiled in 1921), formal lawns designed by architect James Miller, and the Category B listed Christie Park Lodge. Access and Facilities Location: Situated on Middleton Street, Alexandria (G83 0DF). Entrance Points: The main entrance is on Main Street, leading past the Lodge, with another entrance near the Vale of Leven Bowling Club. Activities: The park features a children’s play area with climbing frames and swings, as well as extensive walking paths through its 9 acres of formal gardens and 5 acres of woodland. Parking: Car parking is available near the entrance by the bowling club. Timings Park Hours: While the park itself generally offers open access for walkers and visitors during daylight hours, specific facilities like the main car park may have set hours (typically 9:00 AM to 6:30 PM) Note  Not a comercial or promotional content but to promote trave and tourisim. In 1831, soldiers marched in perfect step across a bridge and the rhythm made it collapse. That actually happened. On April 12, 1831, the Broughton Suspension Bridge over the River Irwell near Salford, England, collapsed under a column of marching soldiers. A detachment of about 74 men from the 60th Rifle Corps was returning to barracks, marching four abreast, when they felt the iron bridge start to bounce in rhythm with their steps. Some found it amusing and deliberately "humoured it," stamping in time, which amplified the vibration until a bolt failed and the bridge gave way. The river below was shallow, so men were injured but nobody died. The incident led the British Army to order troops to "break step" when crossing bridges — a practice still followed today. 📖 Source: Wikipedia — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broughton_Suspension_Bridge #history #thatactuallyhappened #engineering #fyp created by thatactuallyhappened with thatactuallyhappened's Originalton

This is the largest keep in Scotland - Alloa Tower and it's around 700 years old! Built by the Erskines, it sat near a ferry across the River Forth as a clear show of strength. You can even see where the old entrance could only be reached by ladder for extra defense! Fortunately, there's a more accessible front door today and you can get inside thanks to the National Trust for Scotland Being so close to Stirling Castle and owned by a family as important as the Erskine Earls of Mar meant that Alloa saw plenty of royal visitors. Mary Queen of Scots and James VI were both regular guests. It was home to the infamous leader of the 1715 Jacobite Rising, John Erskine, nicknamed Bobbing John due to his shifting allegiances. Not wanting to live in a draughty towerhouse anymore, he added a large, comfortable mansion here in 1710. Sadly, that was destroyed by fire, but the Tower survived unscathed. Clearly, those old, thick stone walls came in handy! #Scotland #VisitScotland #Clackmannashire #CastlesOfScotland #ScottishCastles #ScotlandIsNow  created by Scotland's Stories - Graeme with Tony Anderson's The King

The abandoned walled garden within the grounds of what was Alloa House on the Mar Estate has been brought back to life through the hard work and hope invested by the local community group at Wimpy Park, who have been campaigning and fundraising since 2017. Combined with local council and third sector support, they secured a long term-lease with a view to re-establishing a garden, as well as play areas for children and young people over a phased period. A massive boost to their efforts came in summer 2021 from the National Lottery Community Fund investment. Gean House, or The Gean, is an early 20th-century Arts and Crafts style mansion, located on Tullibody Road, Alloa, Scotland. It was owned and used as a venue for events but has now been restored to a private residence since October 2018.    In November 1911, Alexander Forrester-Paton, of Inglewood House, Alloa, purchased 30 acres (12 ha) of land from the Earl of Mar and Kellie, for £6,220. His intention was to "erect and complete in a satisfactory manner a Mansion House and relative Offices."[citation needed] Alexander Forrester-Paton was the managing director of the Alloa-based firm of Patons, the family business founded by his grandfather to manufacture woollen yarn. Some 16 years earlier, Alexander had purchased land from the Earl to build his own family home at nearby Inglewood. Alexander Forrester-Paton also owned large estates in Clackmannanshire, and built several other buildings, such as Cowdenpark, where he lived. Gean House was to be built as a wedding gift for Alexander's eldest son, also named Alexander, who worked in the family business. Plans were commissioned from William Kerr (1866–1940), partner in the local firm of John Melvin & Sons,an architect previously engaged to design Patons' headquarters at Kilncraigs in Alloa. The Gean House commission was not confined to the erection of one building. Kerr's task was to design and construct a mini-estate, including north, south and east lodges, a walled garden, glasshouses and a garage. #drone #scotland #alloa #geanhouse #mavic3classic @DJI 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿👍🏻🔵🔴🔵👍🏻🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿🏕️🧗 #drone #scotland #mavic3classic #geanhouse #outdoors #drones #alloa  created by ramsayoutdoors🏕️ with Øneheart & reidenshi's snowfall

Alloa Town Hall is a municipal building in Marshill, Alloa, Scotland. The structure, which was the meeting place of Alloa Burgh Council, is a Category C listed building. Until the late 19th century Alloa lacked a public hall capable of accommodating a large number of people,so when a director of John Paton Son and Co., John Thomson Paton, offered to pay for a town hall as a gift to the town,burgh leaders agreed to accept the offer: the site they selected was occupied by some large private houses. The Speirs Centre was built as Alloa's swimming pool in 1895 and was designed by Sir John Burnet of Glasgow. Things to do in Stirling ⚔️🏰 Stirling is a city we visit allll the time. I love its quaintness, its history, and strolling around the streets with a coffee in hand, marvelling at the details of the architecture.  We always base ourselves at @Menstrie Castle Stay (ad/gifted) nearby in the village of Menstrie. There are three apartments you can choose from- each sleeping between 2-6 guests.  One of my favourite things to do is wander the Old Town, exploring Stirling Castle, the Old Town Cemetery and the Church of the Holy Rude.  There are so many amazing stories tucked away in the walls of these buildings, and if you love haunted places, there are plenty of ghostly tales too!  At Cambuskenneth Abbey, you can see the grave of Scottish King James III and Queen Margaret. This is a quiet place away from the hustle and bustle of the city, and one of my favourite hidden gems.  The Battle of Bannockburn Visitor Centre is excellent if you want to learn more about the battle led by Robert the Bruce. This is the largest keep in Scotland - Alloa Tower and it's around 700 years old! Built by the Erskines, it sat near a ferry across the River Forth as a clear show of strength. You can even see where the old entrance could only be reached by ladder for extra defense! Fortunately, there's a more accessible front door today and you can get inside thanks to the National Trust for Scotland Being so close to Stirling Castle and owned by a family as important as the Erskine Earls of Mar meant that Alloa saw plenty of royal visitors. Mary Queen of Scots and James VI were both regular guests. It was home to the infamous leader of the 1715 Jacobite Rising, John Erskine, nicknamed Bobbing John due to his shifting allegiances. Not wanting to live in a draughty towerhouse anymore, he added a large, comfortable mansion here in 1710. Sadly, that was destroyed by fire, but the Tower survived unscathed. Clearly, those old, thick stone walls came in handy! #Scotland #VisitScotland #Clackmannashire #CastlesOfScotland #ScottishCastles #ScotlandIsNow  created by Scotland's Stories - Graeme with Tony Anderson's The King

A few months ago, I was approached by St Mungo’s Primary in Alloa after the school moved into its new premises within Alloa Academy. As part of that transition, they wanted a way to establish their identity in the new space and create something that felt uniquely theirs. The aim was to create a large-scale mural that celebrated the school community while brightening the grounds and giving pupils a stronger sense of ownership over their surroundings. The pupils came up with ideas that best represented the school’s values and ethos. St Mungo’s is a colourful place, so their rainbow values became a key part of the design. They also shared their mottos, We Grow Together and Rooted in Love, which inspired imagery of flowers, plants and wildlife throughout the piece. Using sketches created by the pupils, I developed a design that could be realised on a large scale while staying true to their ideas. Over two weeks, I painted the mural in my studio across two plywood panels measuring 8 x 8 ft when joined together, using a combination of spray paint, emulsion and acrylics. To give the work a more organic feel, I also cut around the edges rather than leaving it as a simple square panel. The mural was installed last week and has now been unveiled for the school community to enjoy. I’m really pleased with how it turned out, and it’s been great to hear such positive feedback from pupils, staff and parents. A huge thank you to Planet Youth Scotland for funding the project. Planet Youth Scotland works to improve the health, wellbeing and relationships of young people by preventing substance use and promoting positive environments. It was great to contribute to that mission through this artwork and help create something that the school community can enjoy for years to come. I’d also like to thank the Clackmannanshire Family Wellbeing Partnership and St Mungo’s Primary for all their support in helping make the project a reality! created by Kyle Blain Art with Sam Fender & Olivia Dean's Rein Me In

Day 59: A Walk A Day 📍 Alloway Tunnel Project, Alloway, Ayr, KA7 4NH 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿 The Alloway Tunnel project aimed to transform a disused, graffiti-covered railway tunnel into a community space with a large, hand-painted mural, inspired by the successful transformation of the Colinton Tunnel in Edinburgh. The project, led by muralist Chris Rutterford, focuses on celebrating Ayrshire's rich heritage, particularly the legacy of Robert Burns, and involves community participation! You can either park at The Robert Burns Birthplace Museum, Murdoch’s Lone, Alloway, KA7 4PQ (where I did notice has its own bus stop so I’m guessing you can get a bus from the bus station straight to it) or park around the back at the Rugby Club (the museum car park closes at 5pm).  From there just cross the road and stick left at the bottom of the lane and within minutes you’ll reach the railway tunnel 😍 The walk is pram and wheelchair friendly and you can spend a fair bit of time admiring the individual murals and the attention to detail which is remarkably impressive ❤️ The Alloway Railway Tunnel Project is certainly a work of art that has to be seen to be fully appreciated 💙🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿 #alloway #tunnel #allowaytunnel #allowaytunnelproject #ayr #ayrshirewalks #glasgowwalks #ayrshire #railwaytunnel #muralist #mural #artworkontiktok #scotland #visitscotland #beautifulscotland #robertburns #poet #poetry #poetlover #rabbieburns #auldlangsyne  created by ✨€mma - Who Knew✨ with JAPAN NEWS's nhạc nền - 8D Music 🎧

A wonderfully unusual vintage locket-style book pendant, created as a souvenir of Burns Cottage in Alloway, Scotland, the birthplace of Scotland’s national poet, Robert Burns. Burns memorabilia (often called “Burnsiana”) was made to celebrate the life and birthplace of Robert Burns. Formed as a small hinged book, the front is decorated with an enamel thistle in green and purple tones. The thistle, long a symbol of Scotland’s resilience and pride, gives the piece an immediate sense of national identity and heritage. #scottishjewellery  #scotland #goldlocket #thistles  created by dearrosewithlove with Danilo Boccato's Cliffs of Scotland

Day 60: A Walk A Day 📍 Greenan Castle, Alloway, Ayr, KA7 4JU 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿 If you’re down at Alloway checking out the Alloway Railway Tunnel Project (see day 59 of my walks) and you have an hour or two to spare then just one mile along the road you’ll find this beauty…..Greenan Castle 😍 As you make your way up from the tunnel you’ll come to a cross roads where you’ll find the Auld Kirk. The Alloway Auld Kirk, which dates back to the 16th century, is a church ruin in Alloway celebrated as the scene of the witches' dance in the poem "Tam o' Shanter" by Robert Burns. William Burns, father of the poet, is buried in the graveyard together with his daughter Isabella as well as two of his nieces. History geeks like myself might also want to check out the Cambusdoon Estate on the way as there’s a lovely wee woodland walk that runs alongside the River Doon (I have since googled it!). Greenan Castle is perched on a clifftop at Greenan Shore and is a 16th-century, ruined tower house looking over to the Heads of Ayr, and out to sea towards Arran and the Ailsa Craig. It was originally a fort, built to spot enemies approaching by sea, but was converted to a motte-and-bailey style structure in the 12th century. In the 15th century, the Earls of Ross, Lords of the Isles, built a grand tower house and it later passed into the hands of the Kennedys.  Beside the tower are the remains of a walled courtyard and outbuildings. From this courtyard in May 1602, Sir Thomas Kennedy and a servant rode towards Edinburgh, but in nearby woods were ambushed and killed as revenge for a killing in battle the previous year. The notorious story inspired Sir Walter Scott to write his short play ‘An Ayrshire Tragedy’.  On the return leg I swung by Burns Cottage, the birthplace of the great Robert Burns. This cosy four-room cottage is where Burns lived until the age of seven. He’s further celebrated along the road with the Poet’s Path which links the Robert Burns Museum with Burns Cottage. Along the way you can spot creative ironwork signage crafted by Timorous Beasties, celebrating scenes from Burns’s Tam o’ Shanter. The path is bordered by seasonal plantings. There’s also plenty of wonderful Burns-related artworks to spot as you stroll along. Look out for Kenny Hunter’s decidedly not-so ‘wee mouse’ made from cast iron and, a little further along, Jake Harvey’s larger-than-life granite haggis. Take a rest on our latest sculpture, The Twa Dogs, by artist Sally Matthews! This is a one hour linear walk with the castle being just one mile along from the starting point. I spent a couple of hours down here and on a sunny day it would be amazing to bring the kids with a picnic. The museum has its own bus stop so you could easily get here in public transport and the well maintained paths make it a delight for prams and wheelchair users. Day 60: A Walk A Day 📍 Greenan Castle, Alloway, Ayr, KA7 4JU 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿 If you’re down at Alloway checking out the Alloway Railway Tunnel Project (see day 59 of my walks) and you have an hour or two to spare then just one mile along the road you’ll find this beauty…..Greenan Castle 😍 As you make your way up from the tunnel you’ll come to a cross roads where you’ll find the Auld Kirk. The Alloway Auld Kirk, which dates back to the 16th century, is a church ruin in Alloway celebrated as the scene of the witches' dance in the poem "Tam o' Shanter" by Robert Burns. William Burns, father of the poet, is buried in the graveyard together with his daughter Isabella as well as two of his nieces. History geeks like myself might also want to check out the Cambusdoon Estate on the way as there’s a lovely wee woodland walk that runs alongside the River Doon (I have since googled it!). Greenan Castle is perched on a clifftop at Greenan Shore and is a 16th-century, ruined tower house looking over to the Heads of Ayr, and out to sea towards Arran and the Ailsa Craig. It was originally a fort, built to spot enemies approaching by sea, but was converted to a motte-and-bailey style structure in the 12th century. In the 15th century, the Earls of Ross, Lords of the Isles, built a grand tower house and it later passed into the hands of the Kennedys.  Beside the tower are the remains of a walled courtyard and outbuildings. From this courtyard in May 1602, Sir Thomas Kennedy and a servant rode towards Edinburgh, but in nearby woods were ambushed and killed as revenge for a killing in battle the previous year. The notorious story inspired Sir Walter Scott to write his short play ‘An Ayrshire Tragedy’.  On the return leg I swung by Burns Cottage, the birthplace of the great Robert Burns. This cosy four-room cottage is where Burns lived until the age of seven. He’s further celebrated along the road with the Poet’s Path which links the Robert Burns Museum with Burns Cottage. Along the way you can spot creative ironwork signage crafted by Timorous Beasties, celebrating scenes from Burns’s Tam o’ Shanter. The path is bordered by seasonal plantings. There’s also plenty of wonderful Burns-related artworks to spot as you stroll along. Look out for Kenny Hunter’s decidedly not-so ‘wee mouse’ made from cast iron and, a little further along, Jake Harvey’s larger-than-life granite haggis. Take a rest on our latest sculpture, The Twa Dogs, by artist Sally Matthews! This is a one hour linear walk with the castle being just one mile along from the starting point. I spent a couple of hours down here and on a sunny day it would be amazing to bring the kids with a picnic. The museum has its own bus stop so you could easily get here in public transport and the well maintained paths make it a delight for prams and wheelchair users. With Burns Night approaching, come for a Wee Wander around the birthplace of Robert Burns in Alloway! This wee thatched building built by Burns' father, is where Scotland's National poet was born and raised alongside 3 of his 6 siblings. Must have been a tight squeeze considering it's half cottage and half barn! Head out the door and up Poets Path to be faced with a great big, haggis - the chieftain of the pudding race! Keep your eyes open for witches and warlocks in a dance at Auld Alloway Kirk or head to the Brig o Doon to see if Maggie's tail is lying about on the cobblestones... Then to the grand Burns Monument by way of a Red, Red Rose. The views from the top are fantastic and if you need refreshment then Tam o Shanter and Souter Johnny aren't far away. Lastly, into the Burns Museum to explore items from the bard's life and you might even spot a wee, sleekit cowering timorous beastie. A trip to Alloway is highly recommended for all fans of Robert Burns, but there are lots more places to visit linked with the bard! His home with Jean Armour at Mauchline, the farm he built at Ellisland is amazing and in Dumfries you can visit his Mausoleum or sit in his chair at the Globe Inn! Tam O’ Shanter is a legendary poem written by Robert Burns.  It focuses on the main character, Tam, as he travels home from the pub. On the way, he has a supernatural encounter riding past the local church. Through the window, Tam sees witches and warlocks dancing a ceilidh, while the Devil himself plays the bagpipes. The church had a reputation for being haunted before this, but it’s decorated with all sorts of gory, gruesome artefacts. Tam drunkenly calls out to a witch whom had caught his eye “Weel done Cutty-Sark” referring to her revealing clothing. All those witches and creatures at the dance started to chase after him. Tam kicks his horse Meg and tries to get to the River Doon and cross it before he’s caught. Tam and Meg reach the bridge, however poor Meg loses her tail in the process. Some might say the moral of the story it’s to be mindful of the consequences our actions might have. Take to the skies above Arbroath Signal Tower Museum, a hidden gem on Scotland’s stunning east coast. 🏛️✨ Built in 1813, this striking white building was designed as the shore station for the Bell Rock Lighthouse, the world’s oldest surviving sea-washed lighthouse. The Signal Tower served as the hub for lighthouse keepers and their families, offering a vital link to the maritime world. Today, it stands as a testament to Scotland’s rich maritime heritage, housing fascinating exhibitions about lighthouse technology, the history of Bell Rock, and life on the Angus coast. Situated near Arbroath’s picturesque harbor, the museum offers breathtaking views of the North Sea and provides a perfect blend of history, architecture, and natural beauty. Nestled just outside the seaside town of Arbroath, Hospitalfield House is one of Scotland’s most unique historic buildings — and a hidden treasure for lovers of art, architecture, and quiet beauty. Originally founded as a medieval hospice, the house was transformed in the 19th century by artist and philanthropist Patrick Allan-Fraser into a Gothic Revival masterpiece and artistic retreat. Today, its ornate interiors, stained glass, carved stone, and walled gardens reflect a deep commitment to creativity and heritage. Still an active arts centre, Hospitalfield continues to support artists-in-residence and exhibitions — blending Scotland’s past with its living creative spirit. With regular house and garden tours there is so much to see. There is also a lovely cafe serving superb food within the walled garden. #HospitalfieldHouse #Arbroath #ScottishArchitecture #HistoricScotland #HiddenScotland #ScotlandTravel #GothicRevival #ArtAndHistory #AngusScotland #CulturalScotland created by Stepdive with Stepdive's original sound

William Wallace’s connection to Ardrossan Castle is defined by one of the more gruesome and enduring legends of the Scottish Wars of Independence. Known as "Wallace's Larder," the tale centers on a daring stratagem used to recapture the stronghold from English forces in the late 13th century. ​According to local lore and the writings of the minstrel Blind Harry, Wallace and his men set fire to a group of nearby buildings to lure the English garrison out of the castle. As the soldiers rushed out to extinguish the flames, Wallace’s party ambushed them, swiftly taking control of the gates. ​The climax of the story is particularly grim, ​After defeating the soldiers, the Scots threw the bodies of the slain English garrison into the castle’s lightless dungeon vault. ​Wallace allegedly quipped that the pile of bodies would serve as a "larder" (a room for storing meat) for the English, as he intended to leave them there to rot while he dismantled the castle’s defenses. ​While the "Larder" story leans heavily into the romanticized brutality of later chronicles, Ardrossan was undoubtedly a strategic site during this era. #historytime #scotland #castle #fyp #folklore  created by Man and cam 📸 with Mizmo's Hello

Negotiations to bring Ardrossan Harbour into public ownership have been completed, the Transport Secretary has said. The facility is currently owned by Peel Ports, but has been sought by the Scottish Government’s ferry procurement arm Caledonian Maritime Assets Limited (CMAL) since it became clear two new ferries serving the route between the mainland and the Isle of Arran would not be able to dock there. The Glen Sannox entered service last year with its sister ship, the Glen Rosa, due to be handed over at the end of 2026. As a result with the issues at the port, ferries have had to operate from Troon – down the Ayrshire coast – leaving Ardrossan without a ferry service for more than 18 months while the aging Caledonian Isles was out of service. While it is not yet clear how much the Government has paid for the harbour, substantial work is expected to be required to make it suitable for the new ferries. #news #shorts #politics #boat #ferry  #currentaffairs created by STV News with STV News's original sound - STV News

The former Seafield House (or Seafield Tower) in Ardrossan, seen here is one of the last great mansions of the Three Towns. Originally built in 1820, it was rebuilt to its current design (Scottish Baronial) in 1858. In the mid 20th century it became Seafield Residential School, and in 2004 became Quarriers Seafield School. Quarriers closed the school in 2014, and in 2017 a massive fire gutted much of the building, resulting in the demolition of all non-listed extensions etc. The old house has pretty much lay derelict ever since. #ardrossan #urbex #abandoned #urbanexploring #fyp  created by ⛧⸸ Mo Mayhem ⸸⛧ with STAKILLAZ's ?К0N3Ц..

Come with me… to one of Scotland’s most beautiful castles… where the stones have witnessed centuries of bloodshed.” Standing proudly over Brodick Bay on the Isle of Arran, this castle may look peaceful today… …but it was built for war. For more than 700 years, Brodick Castle has been fought over by kings, invaded by armies, and stained by the brutality of medieval Scotland. During the Wars of Scottish Independence, Arran became a strategic prize. Whoever controlled Brodick controlled the gateway through the Firth of Clyde. The castle changed hands time and time again… Scottish. English. Scottish. English. Every siege meant broken walls… shattered lives… and the screams of men who would never leave these grounds alive. The powerful Hamilton family eventually claimed Brodick as their stronghold, but peace was always fragile. Feuds, clan rivalries and political betrayals haunted these halls for centuries. Imagine standing here on a stormy night… The crash of waves below… The clash of steel… The smell of smoke… And the cries of wounded soldiers echoing through the darkness. It’s said that beneath the tranquil gardens and elegant rooms lies a history written not with ink… …but with blood. Today, visitors come for the views. But if these ancient walls could speak… they wouldn’t tell fairy tales. They’d tell stories of war… betrayal… and death. Trying to explore more of what’s right on my doorstep. Today I walked from Cullaloe Woods along the old North Road, dating back to the 16th century, to visit Auchtertool Holy Well — an ancient and historically significant water source. It was once used for baptisms and for the celebration of mass, and served as a stopping point for pilgrims travelling between Inchcolm and St Andrews. The well itself was a bit of a disappointment, if I’m honest, but the journey there more than made up for it. A few peaceful hours spent wandering through woodland and plantation, stopping along the way for a bit of forest bathing — sometimes the path is the real destination. #scotland  #auchtertool  #heritage  #aberdour  #treckking  created by Mother Nature's Distraction with DID YOU KNOW's original sound - Keith_kate

I almost didn’t go to Kincardine. It kept coming up in conversations; someone would mention it in passing, or I’d see a photo of that lighthouse at golden hour and think “I should go there sometime.” And then I’d forget about it and plan something else instead. I finally went last Summer. And I’ve been thinking about it ever since. There’s something about this town that’s hard to explain. It’s not trying to be anything other than what it is, a small lakeside town with Scottish roots, a lighthouse that’s been standing since 1880, beaches that face west so every single evening turns into something worth stopping for, and a community that genuinely seems to love where it lives. The full guide is in the reel : where to start your morning, which lighthouse to visit, where to eat, where to stay, and the one sunset experience that I genuinely was not prepared for. Kincardine is about two and a half hours from Toronto and one hour from Kitchener, so save this for your summer planning. 🔖 Have you been to Kincardine before?  created by Marie | Ontario Wanderer 🇨🇦 with Marie | Ontario Wanderer 🇨🇦's original sound

think I need to bring these videos back 👀 • Tullibardine Chapel, Outlander ep. 2x11 ‘Vengeance is Mine’ • Dating as far back as 1446 by Sir David Murray, but extended around 1500 by Sir Andrew Murray, Tullibardine Chapel is a monument to the piety of the Murray family, ancestors of the Dukes of Atholl. It served as a private church of the family until the reformation in 1560. It is one of the very few medieval churches in all of Scotland to have survived the reformation unaltered. It remained the Murray’s burial ground into the 1900s. ✨ Tullibardine Chapel is a 15th century site that survived the Reformation largely unscathed. 🦌 A MUST VISIT IN AVIEMORE! 🦌 We paid a visit to the Cairngorm Reindeer Centre while exploring Aviemore and the Cairngorms, and it’s such a lovely little experience for the family! ❤️ Home to Britain’s only free-ranging herd of reindeer, you can get up close and see some of these amazing animals right here in the Scottish Highlands. 🏔️🦌 We visited the Paddocks & Exhibition, which is a brilliant option if you’ve got younger kids or don’t fancy heading out on the full Hill Trip. ✨ See the reindeer up close 🦌 Learn all about the herd 🧒 Little quiz for the kids 🏔️ Beautiful Cairngorms setting 👨‍👩‍👧‍👦 Great family activity 💰 Really affordable too! The Paddocks & Exhibition usually costs around £5 for adults and £4 for children during the summer, with under 3s FREE.* Definitely one to add to your list if you’re planning a family trip to Aviemore or the Cairngorms! 📍🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿 ⚠️ Always check the Cairngorm Reindeer Centre website before travelling for the latest opening information and availability. 📍PLACES TO TAKE THE KIDS THAT THE WHOLE FAMILY WILL ACTUALLY ENJOY – EPISODE 6 🐻‍❄️🐯 Snow leopard cubs, tigers and polar bears… oh my! 🤍 If you’re looking for an unforgettable family day out in the Scottish Highlands, then @Highland Wildlife Park just outside Aviemore, needs to be on your list! From the moment we arrived, Finn couldn’t wait to start exploring with his map in hand, and there was so much to see. The highlight of our day had to be seeing not one, but TWO polar bears up close. They’re absolutely incredible to watch and one of the main reasons so many families visit. We also felt incredibly lucky to catch a glimpse of the tiny snow leopard cubs. They were so cute, playful and definitely one of those moments that makes your whole day. We also spotted the magnificent Amur tigers, Scottish wildcats, Japanese macaques and so many other amazing animals along the way. One thing I’d really recommend is looking into the Royal Zoological Society of Scotland membership. It gives you unlimited entry to Highland Wildlife Park and Edinburgh Zoo, making it fantastic value if you love family days out and plan to visit more than once throughout the year. We spent hours wandering around, learning about the animals and making memories together, and it’s definitely one of those places that both kids and adults genuinely enjoy. 📍 Highland Wildlife Park, Kincraig (near Aviemore), Cairngorms National Park 💙 Save this for your next trip to the Highlands and tag someone who’d love this family day out! #HighlandWildlifePark #Aviemore #FamilyDaysOut #ScotlandWithKids #VisitScotland  created by Mum who runs with Mum who runs's original sound

The project, led by muralist Chris Rutterford, focuses on celebrating Ayrshire's rich heritage, particularly the legacy of Robert Burns, and involves community participation! Doon at the Auld Brig in Ayr — stoaps like thir hae seen mair than a wheen o’ stories. A braw wee daunder alang the watter  Legend has it that the first bridge was founded by a pair of sisters, one of whom was mourning her drowned lover. Their likenesses were carved into the eastern parapet of the Brig, and could still be seen in the Victorian era.  Due to its weakening structure over the centuries, the Auld Brig has been frequently repaired; it was joined in 1788 by the New Brig 100 yards downstream.  Both bridges are commemorated in Robert Burns's poem, 'The Brigs o' Ayr. The poem describes an argument between the two bridges, in which the Auld Brig predicts that it shall remain standing long after the New Brig has gone - a prediction which actually came true! The New Brig had to be demolished after a severe storm in 1879. The present New Bridge is a complete rebuild, while the Old Bridge of Ayr is still standing. #AuldBrig #AyrshireBlether #ayr #robertburns #rabbieburns #AyrScotland #HiddenGems #HistoricViews #oldbridge  created by Mr Scotland with Litne's Celtic

A visit yesterday to the Kirk that Cromwell built. The Auld Kirk of Ayr stands where a Franciscan friary—the Greyfriars of Ayr—once stood, founded before 1230. Their cloister looked over the River Ayr, close to the harbour and the medieval St John’s Church, where Robert the Bruce held his famous Parliament in 1315 to confirm the royal succession. When the Reformation came in 1560, the friars’ buildings were stripped and the site reused; by 1654, a new T-plan kirk rose from the friary stones. Cromwell’s troops occupied nearby St John’s, turning it into a citadel. The old parish moved uphill to this new kirk, still marked by its 1656 lychgate. Later, the Burns family worshipped here after Alloway parish was annexed to Ayr the same pews once filled by the masons who built it from monastic rubble. #Ayr #AuldKirk #Greyfriars #Covenanters #StJohnsTower                                  📜🦄🏛️⚖️ David E Easson, Medieval Religious Houses: Scotland (Longman 1957) p 83 — lists Ayr’s Franciscan (Greyfriar) friary among the early thirteenth-century foundations. 💻🦄🏛️⚖️ Canmore (Historic Environment Scotland), ‘Greyfriars, Ayr’ https://canmore.org.uk/site/41148/ayr-greyfriars (accessed 9 Nov 2025) — records foundation before 1230 and later reuse of masonry in Auld Kirk. 💻🦄🏛️ Scotland’s Churches Trust, ‘The Auld Kirk of Ayr’ https://www.scotlandschurchestrust.org.uk/church/the-auld-kirk-of-ayr/ — details 1654 construction, 1656 lychgate, and links. created by BàrdLucy ☘️ 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿 with BàrdLucy ☘️ 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿's original sound

A bid to reinstate diving facilities at Ayr’s Citadel Leisure Centre, using £70,000 of council reserves for one year, is set to go before South Ayrshire Council this week. The motion has been lodged by Labour group leader, Councillor Duncan Townson and seconded by Councillor Cameron Ramsay, and calls on the local authority to reverse an earlier decision to remove diving provision at the pool. Councillors are being asked to agree to reconsider the previous decision and temporarily restore diving from the three and five-metre platforms for one year. If you grew up in Scotland during the 1990s or early 2000s, there’s a good chance Loudoun Castle was part of your childhood. Opened in 1995 within the historic Loudoun Castle estate, it quickly became one of Scotland’s best-loved family theme parks. But after declining visitor numbers and the tragic death of an 18-year-old ride operator in 2007, the park was deemed no longer economically viable and closed permanently in September 2010. Today, the 610-acre estate remains private property. Many of the rides have been removed or left to decay, while the historic castle itself—whose oldest surviving parts date back to the 15th century—remains hidden behind locked gates. Protected as a Category A listed building, it is rarely seen by the public. For years, there have been proposals to redevelop the estate, but none have become reality. Day 52: A Walk A Day 📍 Rozelle Estate, Ayr, KA7 4NQ Rozelle Estate is a stunning woodland trail taking you a circular walk around the outskirts of the estate where you’ll find the beautiful WW1 rememberance woodland. This was created to for the centenary commemoration of the fallen hero’s of WW1 and features chainsaw tree carvings amongst other sculptures 😍 The centre features a tearoom and museum which is free and is open Monday-Saturday, 10am to 5pm ❤️ At the centre of the trail is a massive grass area that’s perfect for a picnic or games with the kids or just a spot of sunbathing 😎 I can’t NOT mention the number of squirrels I saw 😍 they were EVERYWHERE!!! Ballater Station lies at the Royal Deeside in Aberdeenshire, Scotland. Though no longer an active railway hub, this charming former station holds a rich history and exudes a captivating nostalgia. Ballater Station was built in 1886, and it served as the grand gateway to Balmoral Castle, the Scottish retreat of the British Royal Family. Designed by renowned architect Andrew Maitland, the station boasted a majestic presence with its granite facade, ornate clock tower, and spacious platforms. A dedicated Royal Waiting Room, adorned with intricate wood carvings and stained-glass windows, awaited the arrival of the monarchs. Sadly, the last train pulled out of Ballater in 1966, marking the end of an era. But the station's story wasn't over yet. In the 1980s, a dedicated community effort launched a restoration project, bringing the station back to its former glory. Today, the beautifully restored Ballater Station stands as a testament to this unwavering spirit. The building now houses the bustling Ballater iCentre, a treasure trove of information for visitors exploring Royal Deeside, and housing a variety of shops, cafes, and boutiques. Visitors can browse through unique local crafts, enjoy a cup of tea in a cozy cafe, or simply take in the scenic views of the surrounding hills and forests. A visit to Ballater Station is more than just a trip down memory lane. It's a chance to step into a bygone era, to imagine the excitement of royal arrivals and the bustle of bygone travelers. Whether you're a history buff, a train enthusiast, or simply seeking a captivating day trip, Ballater Station promises an experience that is both grand and heartwarming.  So, pack your bags, board the (imaginary) train, and step back in time to this enchanting corner of Scotland. The Glen Tanar Schoolhouse ​The buildings you captured are the former Glen Tanar School and Schoolhouse. ​The Visionary: The estate was transformed in the late 19th century by Sir William Cunliffe Brooks, a Manchester banker and MP who bought the land in 1865. He turned the area into a "model estate," employing architect George Truefitt to design numerous buildings.  ​The Architecture: Truefitt was Brooks' preferred architect, and the schoolhouse reflects the distinct, high-quality Victorian granite stonework seen throughout the estate. These structures were built not just as utilitarian buildings, but as part of an intentionally curated landscape that blends into the natural surroundings of the glen.The drinking fountain is one of many "inscribed stones" and memorials hidden throughout the estate. ​The Occasion: It was built to commemorate Queen Victoria’s Diamond Jubilee in 1897.  ​The Message: Sir William Cunliffe Brooks had a unique habit of placing these stones to offer messages to travelers. He often used these fountains to promote the virtue of drinking water over alcohol—a common Victorian moral stance. ​The Inscription: You can see the dedication to Queen Victoria, noting her 60-year reign from 1837–1897. The phrasing on the stone is classic "Brooks-style" messaging, designed to make a weary traveler stop, reflect, and appreciate the "gift" of fresh water. ​The Wellingtonia Tree ​This tree is a perfect companion to the school and well, as it ties back to the same historic timeline. ​The Connection: Like the drinking well, this Wellingtonia (Giant Sequoia) was planted in 1897 to celebrate the Diamond Jubilee of Queen Victoria.  ​Victorian Fashion: Planting exotic conifers like Wellingtonias was very popular on grand Scottish estates during the Victorian era. It was a way for owners to demonstrate their wealth and connection to the global reach of the British Empire. Today, it stands as a living monument to that same 1897 celebration you see on the well. "Victorian Time Capsule." Both the schoolhouse and the tree were created as part of the same 1897 Jubilee efforts, showing how the estate was developed to be both functional (the school) and monumental (the tree and the well) at the same time. ​#ShotsOTheShire #fyp  #GlenTanar #AbandonedScotland #VictorianHistory    created by Shots 'o' The Shire with ⭐️👁️🇬🇧BILLIONAIREPROPHETESS's original sound

Knock Castle is a four-story tower house ruin near Ballater in Aberdeenshire, Scotland, dating to around 1600. It was granted to the Gordons of Abergeldie by the 4th Earl of Huntly after the Battle of Corrichie in 1562, where Huntly’s forces fought those of Mary Queen of Scots. The site is tied to a local legend involving a violent feud with Clan Forbes, in which all seven Gordon sons were killed over a peat-cutting dispute. Their father, Alexander Gordon, is said to have died by falling down the stairs after hearing the news from a servant who witnessed the bodies. The Forbes laird was executed for the attack and his lands were forfeited to Abergeldie.  #lightfantasy #darkfantasy #renaissance #history #scottishhistory #Scotland #scotlandtravel #scotlandtravel #Summer #visitscotland #cottagecore #fyp #foryoupage #UK #mythology #mythology #scottishcountryside #nature  #medievaltiktok #fantasy  created by KelseyTheStrange with Joel Sunny's Luminary

A seventh century site by a St Nathalan was abandoned 1798 when it merged with Glenmuick and Glengairn and a new parish built in Ballater.St Nathalan is said to be buried here. Nineteenth century subdivided into three prominent burial Isles for the Farquharsons Grants and Emslies.Still used today for burials.Evidence of seventh to ninth centurie burials here. Tullich Pictish Stones.Walkthrough. Tullich kirkyard. Ballater. A set of twenty seven carved stones at this site what an eye-catcher. Dating around sixth to ninth century AD.Showing a transitional time moving picts from pagan society to christian.St Nathalan the founder of the kirk and the site and whom had strong links here died in the year AD678. This was a key location for christian missionaries at the time spreading faith from West to East Scotland. Most of the stones were found right here but being used as building blocks in the old kirk itself until being all rediscovered in the nineteenth century. There is as stated at the site one Pictish class one Stone dating from seven hundred AD where most of the other stones were said to be early christian grave markers holding christian symbols. I have a wee post or two up on the kirk itself so check out @shotsotheshire tick-tock Instagram YouTube. Thank you for all your support its making the journey mean something. Walled Garden🌺🌱  Balloch Castle Country Park🏰🌳 This carefully designed and well-maintained garden was built in 1808, around the same time as Balloch Castle.  Originally called the Kitchen Garden, its layout has not altered in over 200 years. This category B listed building would’ve provided the estate with an array of fruits,  vegetables and flowers. Grapevines, peach trees and pot plants would have been grown here, along with small fruits and vegetables. Greenhouses and potting sheds were based on the inside and outskirts of the garden walls. One greenhouse on the north wall having grapevines and another on the east wall containing peach trees.  The tall stone walls and towering woodland adjacent would’ve provided protection and shelter for the delicate plants from the severe Scottish gales.  It is known that during WW2 the fruit and vegetables grown here aided in harsh rationing and shortages of the war.  The garden had two gardeners inhabiting two small houses and a bothy built onto the north east corner, outside of the walls. Both of these houses had windows facing into the garden, so they could keep surveillance of anyone trying to make off with the produce. These houses were described as “the most dismal houses on the estate”  In the 1960’s a gas cooking accident occurred and both houses were set ablaze and destroyed. In the early 1990’s both the houses and bothy were removed due to being unsafe.  During the next decade, the Walled Gardens had fallen into a state of despair and in 2003 the park received a £2.4m restoration grant with the Walled Garden returning to its former glory. #lochlomond #ballochcastlecountrypark #ballochcastle #walledgarden #scotland  created by BallochParkGuide with moshimo sound design's Chopin Nocturne No. 2 Piano Mono

Balloch sits quietly at the edge of Loch Lomond, where the landscape begins to shift and the hills start to open out toward the Highlands. Close to Glasgow, but it feels a world away.  Paths through Balloch Castle Country Park, soft spring light, and the loch never far - appearing between the trees, then stretching out wide when you least expect it. People gathered along the shoreline, taking their time. Swimming, sitting, wandering. No real sense of urgency to anything. Higher up, the views open out across Loch Lomond and into the Trossachs, wide, still and quietly impressive. Finished with a roast at Balloch House, one of those Sundays that doesn’t ask for much, but leaves you feeling better for it. #lochlomond #balloch #visitscotland #slowsunday #sundayroast  created by Curated Scotland with Dennis Korn's Art of Now (Nature Sounds)
