caption: Loch Lomond for the day 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿☀️ Last week we went a day trip to Loch Lomond and had such a lovely day!  We got the train from Motherwell to Balloch, we had to swap trains at Dalmuir but it was so easy. For myself, Marley and Axel it came to £11.30 for return tickets as we took advantage of the kids for a quid @scotrail  The train takes you right in the centre of Balloch which means all the main attractions are within walking distance. We went to @llsealife which was a great hit with the kids and always one of our favourites to visit when here. Afterwards we headed to @jurassic_grill for some lunch. I have been before with Marley but this was Axel’s first visit, he loves dinosaurs so he really enjoyed all the decor and getting to meet some of the resident dinosaurs 🦕  There were some fun activities for the kids at the shores too, Marley had a go in the inflatable water balls and also on the trampolines. The tokens for these were very reasonable priced!  We finished off our day with some ice cream and then headed back to the station.  There’s so much to do that we didn’t do this time round such as the Loch Lomond bird of prey, mini golf, Go wild which is an outdoor tree top adventure, Balloch country park and of course different boat trips you can take too. 📆 35 years ago, 50,000 Runrig fans crammed into Balloch Castle Country Park, Loch Lomond for an unforgettable night 🎶 🎤🎸🏰🌳 "I'd never seen so many people gathered together in one place... One of the most beautiful walks in Royal Deeside 🌿✨  Starting from Scotly Hill car park in Banchory (postcode AB31 5HU), this stunning circular riverside walk takes around 2 hours and offers some of the very best scenery the area has to offer. Following peaceful woodland paths and the banks of the River Dee, the route is perfect for anyone looking to slow down, enjoy nature, and explore the outdoors at a relaxed pace 🏞️ The walk loops through beautiful forest trails with incredible views across the river, tall Scots pine trees, and quiet natural spaces where you can truly switch off. Keep an eye out for local wildlife along the way too — from birds soaring overhead to squirrels, deer, and salmon in the river if you’re lucky 🦌🐿️🦅 The mix of woodland, flowing water, and fresh Highland air makes this one of the most peaceful and rewarding walks near Banchory. Whether you’re visiting for a weekend escape, walking the dog, or just looking for a scenic route to enjoy with family and friends, this circular walk offers the perfect balance of river views, wildlife, and classic Scottish countryside. After your walk, stop by Banchory Lodge Hotel @banchorylodge for a delicious lunch or coffee overlooking the River Dee 🍽️☕ The perfect way to end a day exploring Royal Deeside. #RoyalDeeside #Banchory #ScotlandWalks #RiverDee #NatureWalk VisitScotland ScottishHighlands WoodlandWalks WildlifeSpotting DogFriendlyWalks WeekendAdventures BanchoryLod created by Aberdeenshire_explorers with Aberdeenshire_explorers's original sound

Just outside Banchory, the Water of Feugh crashes over rock and boulder to meet the River Dee. This is the Falls of Feugh. ​🌲 THIRD TIME LUCKY: Hunting for History in the Hill of Fare trees ⚔️ ​I drove out from home in Banchory today on a mission. To be honest, this was my third time trying to find this exact spot, but today I finally spotted it from the roadside, walked into the trees, and tracked it down—the Corrichie Memorial Stone. ​If you’ve ever driven the B977 or hiked up the Hill of Fare, you’ve probably passed right by this massive 12-foot granite pillar without noticing it. But the bloody, bizarre story behind why it’s hidden here is wild. ​Back on October 28, 1562, these peaceful woods were a brutal battlefield. ​Here is what went down: ​The Clash: It was Mary, Queen of Scots (and her royal army) vs. the ultra-powerful Clan Gordon, led by the Earl of Huntly. Huntly had gone into open rebellion, and Mary marched right up here to the north-east to teach him a lesson. ​The Battle: The Gordons charged downhill into the marshy bog of Corrichie, but the royal forces held the line and utterly crushed them. ​The Weird Death: The Earl of Huntly wasn’t killed by a sword. As he was being captured, the heavily built Earl supposedly had a sudden stroke or heart attack right on his horse and dropped dead on the spot. ​The Ghost Trial: It gets weirder. Months later, his preserved corpse was literally brought to court in Edinburgh to stand trial for treason so the Queen could legally seize his lands! ​The massive stone monument was put up in 1951 to mark the area. If you look closely, it features a haunting Gaelic inscription: "Cuimhnichibh La Coire Fraoichidh" — "Remember the day of Corrichie." ​Standing in the quiet trees today after finally finding it, it’s hard to imagine the chaos that happened right here. If you head further up the hill, you can even find the "Queen's Chair," the rock where Mary Queen of Scots supposedly sat to watch the aftermath. ​Have any of you managed to find the Corrichie Stone, or has it played hide-and-seek with you too? Let me know in the comments! 👇 ​#ShotsOTheShire #Banchory #fyp  #ScottishHistory #HillOfFare      created by Shots 'o' The Shire with Cyber Soundscapes's Eternal Calm

Discover the enchanting Milton of Crathes Castle in Banchory, Scotland! This hidden gem offers a magical escape into history and nature. Wander through beautifully manicured gardens, take in the fresh Scottish air, and marvel at the spectacular 16th-century castle. Step inside and immerse yourself in the captivating tales of the past.  It was said to be home to the enigmatic Lord Milton, a solitary figure cloaked in mystery. People spoke of his generosity and wisdom, as he frequently assisted the villages in their time of need. However, no one had ever seen his face or walked into the bowels of his fortress. A lost traveller took sanctuary at the castle’s gates one stormy night. Surprisingly, the doors swung open to show a vast hall filled with treasures. The traveler met Lord Milton, a kind-hearted soul who had hidden away from the world due to a tragic loss. Lord Milton opened the castle’s doors, inspired by the bravery of the traveller, and invited the locals to rejoice with him. Milton of Creates Castle became a sanctuary of joy, where laughter and friendship echoed through the halls, forever transforming the enigma into a cherished haven of unity. Milton of Crathes Castle offers it everything, from stunning views to exquisite architecture. This is a must-see site for history lovers or those looking for a peaceful escape. From granite gates to rushing waters.🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿 We begin here at the Banchory Bridge of Dee.This granite beauty was built in 1885 replacing an older wooden structure,being one of the most iconic views in the area,looking out over the main stream of the river Dee.From here we will take a wee wander south east towards the feugh. It's a short stunning walk from here but as I'm very slow on the feet iv sped things up for you.Were moving away from the main river to find its largest tributary.you can really feel the landscape closing in as the water gets louder.This area has been a favourite for locals and visitors for centuries,especially those looking to escape the hustle and bustle of town and city life.Arriving at the the bridge of Feugh itself you are hit with what I call a wondrous and amazing site.This stone Bridge dating back to 1790.While Banchory Bridge we just left is grande and wide,this one is narrow and rugged.Being built to withstand the spates a local word for floods when the water of the feugh comes falling down from the forest of Birse. The real magic when looking over the feugh bridge aren't the high vertical drops but the series of powerful rock steps.Its one of the best places in Scotland to see Atlantic salmon.They leap these grounds to reach spawning grounds further upstream.A reminder of just how persistent and wild Scottish nature is. Nip over to Banchory folks and enjoy this wee wonder. See you all out there. Not many people know this place exists, but Cairnpapple Hill is one of the most fascinating ancient sites in Scotland. It’s tucked away near Bathgate in West Lothian and from a distance, it looks like just another quiet hill. Then you reach the top. This spot was sacred for thousands of years. It was first used by Neolithic people for rituals, then as a Bronze Age burial site, and later even early Christians buried their dead here. The coolest part? You can actually go inside the burial cairn. There’s a ladder that takes you down into the stone tomb where people were laid to rest with pots of food and drink for the afterlife. The views from the top are stunning. On a clear day you can see for miles across the landscape. The site is only open in spring and summer and it's looked after by Historic Scotland, so check the opening times before you go. It’s about a 40 minute drive from Edinburgh or a quick 10 minute trip from Bathgate or Linlithgow, with parking nearby. If you’re into ancient history, moody landscapes, or weird hidden gems, definitely save this for your next trip and give us a follow for more Scotland adventures 🙌 #scotland #scotlandtiktok #adventure #archaeology #scotlandtravel #visitscotland  created by Scotlandhiddenadventures with DM Production's Epic Inspiration

Torphichen Preceptory, situated in West Lothian,Scotland, was a medieval establishment founded in the 12th century. It belonged to the Knights Hospitaller of St John of Jerusalem, a contemporaneous order with the Knights Templar. The preceptory played a vital role in the activities of the Hospitallers, including agriculture and military operations. After the Templars' suppression in the 14th century, the property transitioned to the Hospitallers. It holds historical significance as a testament to the presence of both the Hospitallers and Templars in medieval Scotland. . . .  #visitscotland #scottishhistory #scotlandtiktok  #medievalarchitecture #medieval #knightstemplar #westlothian #bathgate #autumn #scotlandtravel #explorescotland  #booktok  #booklover #castles #Scotland #escocia  created by Scotlandhiddenadventures with Tony Anderson's The King

Bearsden Reservoir 🌊🚶 Cubicles? Enormous. Genuinely big enough that you could probably invite a couple of friends in to spectate without anyone feeling cramped. Privacy might be the intended purpose, but there’s certainly no shortage of space. Toilet? Unfortunately, not the cleanest. It looked like it had been waiting a while for some attention, and the overall condition took away from what could have been a decent stop. Toilet paper? Very thin. The sort that tears if you so much as look at it the wrong way, meaning you’ll likely be reaching for far more than you planned. Flush? Surprisingly powerful. One press and it gets straight to work with a satisfying, confident flush. Definitely one of the better features here. Taps? Ice cold. The water comes out absolutely freezing, which is refreshing on a warm day but a bit of a shock if you’re not expecting it.  Cubicle doors? Perfectly functional. They close and lock properly, with plenty of room inside thanks to the oversized cubicles. Hand dryers? A tale of two dryers. One works perfectly well, while the other appears to have given up on life entirely. It’s essentially a 50/50 gamble depending on which one you choose. Overall vibe? A bit of a mixed bag. The huge cubicles and impressively strong flush are definite positives, but they’re let down by the dirty toilet, flimsy toilet paper, freezing cold taps, and the unreliable hand dryer situation. Functional enough if you’re caught short, but there’s definitely room for improvement. Final score: 3.2/10 ⭐️ #fyp #glasgow #toilet #review #walk  created by TheClydesideCrapper with Gummy MusicLab's Ethereal Cosmic Drift

Benbecula (Scottish Gaelic: Beinn na Faoghla, meaning "Mountain of the Ford") is a stunning island in the Outer Hebrides off the west coast of mainland Scotland. ​It serves as a vital geographic and administrative bridge in the Uist island chain, physically connected by road causeways to North Uist and South Uist. Unlike its mountainous neighbors, Benbecula is incredibly flat and low-lying, dotted with hundreds of small freshwater lochs. The highest point is Rueval, a lone hill standing at just 124 meters (407 feet) that offers a panoramic view of the entire island maze. The island's main settlement is Balivanich (Baile a' Mhanaich). It acts as the commercial and administrative center for the Uists, hosting a small airport (with flights to Glasgow and Stornoway), a secondary school, a bank, and local shops. created by Alex in Scotland with FASSounds's Tropical Beats

Benbecula ..The outer Hebrides, Scotland  always get a great sunset here... Benbecula sits between North and South Uist and is linked by causeways, so you can drive island-to-island across the sea. The island name comes from Gaelic: Beinn na Faoghla. Much of the landscape is flat and covered in freshwater lochs and peatland. The beaches here can look tropical on sunny days, with turquoise water and white sand. The area is rich in birdlife — especially geese, waders, and birds of prey. Benbecula played an important role in old clan routes through the Hebrides. The weather during this visit has been a true gift. I never imagined I would have so many days in the high twenties or see 30 degrees showing on my car temperature. The breathtaking beaches, the quiet calm and the space to simply breathe have all made this time even more special. I am so grateful to every beautiful soul who came along to my Silent Counselling group sessions. Introducing new people to the wonders of Silent Counselling, supporting them as they released what they had been carrying and witnessing their profound changes truly makes my soul sing. And woven through it all has been the healing this beautiful place has offered me too. But the best part has been spending most of my days with Mum and Dad. Time together is so precious, and I cherish every moment I have with them. 🤍 Going past Granny’s cottage (Shell Bus) each day and watching it slowly being brought back to life has been incredibly special. It holds so many memories, and there is something deeply moving about seeing life return to a place that is such an important part of my family and my heart. I’ve also loved staying in my sister’s beautiful home and spending my evenings in the hot tub, watching the sky paint a completely new picture every night. Each one has been different, and every one has been breathtaking. During my time here, I also conducted a shamanic ceremony for my ancestors following a sad event that took place. It was deeply personal and powerful, and I’ll share more about that later. There is something about being here that helps me slow down, reconnect with myself and remember what truly matters. I arrived ready to give, but this place and the people I love have given so much back to me. My heart is very full. 🤍 Much love, Fiona ♡ #SilentCounselling #SouthUist #OuterHebrides #AncestralHealing #EmotionalHealing created by Fiona Bowie Silent Counselling with Fiona Bowie Silent Counselling's original sound

Benbecula (Scottish Gaelic: Beinn na Faoghla, meaning "Mountain of the Ford") is a stunning island in the Outer Hebrides off the west coast of mainland Scotland. ​It serves as a vital geographic and administrative bridge in the Uist island chain, physically connected by road causeways to North Uist and South Uist. Unlike its mountainous neighbors, Benbecula is incredibly flat and low-lying, dotted with hundreds of small freshwater lochs. The highest point is Rueval, a lone hill standing at just 124 meters (407 feet) that offers a panoramic view of the entire island maze. The island's main settlement is Balivanich (Baile a' Mhanaich). It acts as the commercial and administrative center for the Uists, hosting a small airport (with flights to Glasgow and Stornoway), a secondary school, a bank, and local shops. created by Alex in Scotland with FASSounds's Tropical Beats

Benbecula ..The outer Hebrides, Scotland  always get a great sunset here... Benbecula sits between North and South Uist and is linked by causeways, so you can drive island-to-island across the sea. The island name comes from Gaelic: Beinn na Faoghla. Much of the landscape is flat and covered in freshwater lochs and peatland. The beaches here can look tropical on sunny days, with turquoise water and white sand. The area is rich in birdlife — especially geese, waders, and birds of prey. Benbecula played an important role in old clan routes through the Hebrides. You can often experience all four seasons in one day on the island. 😁❤️ #Benbecula #OuterHebrides #Scotland #VisitScotland #Hebrides  created by vinnykeenanphotography with vinnykeenanphotography's original sound

There is something deeply comforting about coming home. This was my stomping ground as a child. When the tide was out, I’d be down on the shore picking cockles and mussels. I still remember when this causeway was built, joining Benbecula and South Uist. I’ve always felt deeply connected to this place. No matter where life has taken me, this has always felt like home. For years, I had recurring dreams about trying to cross here. Sometimes it was the old bridge, sometimes the crossing felt dangerous and impossible. The dreams were always filled with a sense of fear and uncertainty. Looking back now, I realise I haven’t had those dreams for years. Whether they reflected old experiences, buried emotions or simply what my mind needed to process, they eventually stopped. It makes me wonder how much we carry inside us without even realising it, and how quietly healing can happen until one day we notice the fear is simply… gone. Standing here tonight, watching the sun set over the waters I knew as a child, I felt the same deep connection I’ve always felt. A short walk from Blairgowrie along the River Ericht will take you to Cargill’s Leap - the point at which the famous Covenanter, Donald Cargill, is said to have escaped Government troops by jumping across the river. Donald Cargill was born in Rattray and was a Presbyterian minister and Covenanter. The Covenanters pledged to maintain their own way of worship following the signing of the National Covenant in 1638.  But during the latter half of Charles II’s reign, Presbyterianism was outlawed by the Scottish Parliament. Ministers who resisted were evicted from the Church.  Cargill, like many other ministers, was forced to hold illegal meetings called ‘conventicles’. These meeting were often broken up by the military and those captured were cruelly treated. On one occasion Cargill managed to escape the troops by leaping a very narrow part of the River Ericht just above Blairgowrie which is now known as Cargill’s Leap.  He was eventually captured in 1681 and taken to Edinburgh where he was found guilty of treason and executed.#foryou #foryoupage #scotland #countryside #river #waterfalls #wilderness #love #naturetiktok #outdoors #TrendTok #fyp  created by ScenicLasy with neozilla's Motivation

Reekie Linn is a dramatic double waterfall on the River Isla, about four miles north of Alyth near Bridge of Craigisla in Angus, Scotland. A short 5‑minute walk from the small car park off the B954 road. Its name comes from Scots: reekie means “smoky/misty” and linn means “pool or cascade,” after the fine spray that shrouds the gorge when the river is high. What makes it especially interesting is the deep, cave‑like plunge pool below called the Black Dub, which local legend says hides a spirit that once appeared to a hiding outlaw as a huge black dog, frightening him into giving himself up! In spate, its two separate drops merge into one thundering fall that surges over sandstone ledges carved out over thousands of years.  #scotland #waterfall #reekielinnwaterfall #blairgowrie #adventure  created by braes and burns with Jhonatan Rodrigues & Piano Sky & Dee Piano's Moment Of Reflection

Did anyone go to Butterfly World as a child?  A trip down memory lane! Once a beloved family attraction, the Butterfly World in Edinburgh (also known as Edinburgh Butterfly and Insect World) was an indoor tropical paradise that transported visitors from the Scottish chill to a vibrant rainforest. It opened its doors in 1984 and was known as the world's longest-running indoor butterfly house, filled with exotic butterflies, reptiles, and other creatures.  For decades, it was a staple for school trips and weekend outings, creating countless happy memories for generations of Scots. However, the attraction's story took a sad turn. After a temporary closure during the COVID-19 pandemic, its owners, Dobbies Garden Centres, announced in July 2021 that it would not be reopening. Citing "exceptionally challenging circumstances," the closure marked the end of an era. The animals were safely rehomed, and the once-thriving sanctuary was left to become an eerie, abandoned shell of its former self, a silent monument to its past. #Abandoned #UrbanExploration #Edinburgh #ButterflyWorld #Scotland #AbandonedPlaces #Urbex #History #ClosedAttraction #nostalgia #travelscotland #lostplaces  created by BabyBear🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿 with daniel.mp3 & Zamaro's childhood

Mavisbank house 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿 Mavisbank House, located near Loanhead in Midlothian, Scotland, is one of the most important early examples of Palladian architecture in Britain. It was designed around 1723 by the eminent Scottish architect William Adam, in partnership with Sir John Clerk of Penicuik—a prominent Enlightenment figure and amateur architect who commissioned it as a private villa. Mavisbank marked a major stylistic shift in Scottish architecture, blending classical Roman elements with the balanced, symmetrical style championed by Palladio. The villa was conceived not merely as a residence but as a symbol of intellectual refinement, serving as a retreat for art, science, and conversation during the Scottish Enlightenment. Over time, the estate’s fortunes changed. In the mid-19th century, Mavisbank was transformed into a private asylum, which was notable for pioneering more humane treatments, such as occupational therapy and time spent in nature—an approach that was advanced for its era. By the early 20th century, however, the building fell into decline. After a fire in 1973 destroyed the interior, the structure became a roofless shell, and it has since been subjected to vandalism, theft, and neglect. Its two wings were demolished, leaving only the central block standing. Despite its dereliction, Mavisbank remains a Grade A–listed building and a key piece of Scotland’s cultural heritage. It has been the subject of preservation campaigns for decades, and in 2024, a significant milestone was reached when the Landmark Trust, in collaboration with Historic Environment Scotland and Midlothian Council, secured £5.3 million from the National Heritage Memorial Fund to acquire and stabilise the property. A compulsory purchase order is underway to bring the house into public ownership, with long-term plans to restore it for community access, education, and heritage-based tourism. If successful, the revival of Mavisbank will be one of the most ambitious and symbolic heritage rescues in the UK. #fyp #viralvideos #Scotland #visitscotland #explorescotland #travelscotland #scottish #scottishtiktok #edinburgh #midlothian #polton #poltonbrae #bonnyrigg #loanhead #abandoned #mavisbankhouse #mavisbank #ruins #abandonedplaces #abandonedhouse #scottishhistory #penicuik #CapCut  created by thebeautyofscotland17 with Secession Studios's Demise of a Nation

Glen Callater is a scenic, glaciated glen south of Braemar in the Cairngorms, featuring the mile-long Loch Callater and a popular, moderate 10km (round-trip) walking track. Known for its dramatic mountain scenery, it acts as a gateway to the high plateau and Munros like Lochnagar, and hosts Callater Stables, a mountain bothy.  Key Features and Highlights: Loch Callater: A high-altitude loch bordered by steep hillsides, popular for hiking, fishing (trout/salmon), and photography, note Visit Cairngorms and VisitAberdeenshire. Callater Stables: An open shelter and mountain bothy (maintained by the MBA) often used by hikers and rescuers, situated near the south end of the loch. Access Route: The main route starts at Auchallater car park, following a well-defined land rover track for roughly 5km to the lodge, offering a relatively accessible entry into the wilder Cairngorms, as described by Walkhighlands and Rhiedorrach Estate. Walking & Mountaineering: The glen provides access to the Munros of Càrn an t-Sagairt Mòr (with plane wreckage), Cairn Bannoch, and Broad Cairn, as detailed on Walkhighlands and in this Steven Fallon article. Jock's Road: A historic, right-of-way path, as shown on the Gazetteer for Scotland website, traverses the glen, offering access towards Glen Doll. Environment: A glacial landscape with steep cliffs and corries at its southern end. #exploring #scotlands #mountains #scenery #viewpoints  @Exploring Scotlands Mountains  created by Exploring My Scotland with lajisfin's som original

Glen Clunie is a scenic glen (valley) and area located near the village of Braemar in the Cairngorms National Park, Aberdeenshire, Scotland.  It is primarily known for its natural beauty, outdoor recreation opportunities, and as the route for a historic military road and the modern A93 public road.  Geography and Location: The glen runs alongside the Clunie Water, a tributary of the River Dee that joins the main river in Braemar. The A93 road, the highest public road in the UK, passes through Glen Clunie on its way from the Cairnwell Pass to Braemar. Outdoor Activities: The area is popular for various outdoor pursuits, including hiking, walking, and cycling, with numerous routes available in the surrounding mountains, such as the Munro, Carn an Tuirc. Historical Significance: A historic military road, built in the mid-18th century by General Caulfield, also passes through the glen and crosses the Clunie Water via the well-preserved, two-arch Fraser's Bridge. Ecology and Conservation: The area is part of a significant river and floodplain restoration project on the Invercauld Estate, involving the planting of native trees and habitat improvement for wildlife. Artistic Inspiration: The tranquil landscape of Glen Clunie has been the subject of several artworks, most notably an 1853 oil painting by the artist Henry Moore, which is housed at the Mercer Art Gallery in Harrogate. #travel #scotland #mountains #scenery #hiking  @Exploring Scotlands Mountains  created by Exploring My Scotland with TranceArk's Wait For You

The Linn of Dee is a famous Highland beauty spot located roughly 6 miles west of Braemar within the Mar Lodge Estate National Nature Reserve. Managed by the National Trust for Scotland, it features a striking 300-metre natural rock gorge where the mighty River Dee narrows down into a rushing torrent. Historically celebrated as a favourite picnic location of Queen Victoria, it serves today as a major gateway for hiking, biking, and exploring the high peaks of the Cairngorms National Park. #scottishsummers #explorescotland  #magicalplaces #forgottenscotland #moss  created by Moss Fairy with shaxzod's оригинальный звук

✨ Hong Kong’s most underrated sunset viewpoint (and the easiest hidden gem to miss!) 🇭🇰🌅 📍Braemar Hill Peak 📸 Search on Google Maps: “Instagram Photo Spot” (this is the exact location in the video. It’s not just the general Braemar Hill Peak location)  🚍 How to get there: 1. Take the MTR to Causeway Bay Station (Exit E) 2. Walk to the minibus stop and catch Green Minibus 25 towards Braemar Hill 3. Get off at Braemar Hill Bus Terminus 4. Walk around 15–20 minutes to reach the viewpoint  🥾 The walk: It’s a short but slightly confusing trail (there are no big signs), so save the Google Maps pin before you go. From the bus stop, follow the path near St. Joan of Arc Secondary School, head up the stairs and follow the trail towards the rocks.  🌅 Best time to visit: Sunset! ⚠️ Bring a torch if you’re walking back after dark as parts of the trail are unlit.
